prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the analysis of nominal rigidities and monetary policy: time-dependent and staggered price and wage setting, and interest-rate policy rules, integrated into a micro-founded theory of monetary policy

statement.case_for: I have moved from B047 to B014. In round 1 I ranked B047 first as a close call, and my main reason for doubting B014 was that the opening trios drew on Taylor, Woodford, Calvo and Galí in different combinations, so I saw no stable attribution. The round-1 files change that. Several members who opened with Galí (Andersson, Fredriksson) moved to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford for reasons about the structure of the contributions. The stated reasons are that Calvo's time-dependent pricing is the primitive of the micro-founded Phillips curve, that Taylor supplied staggered contracts and an estimable policy rule, and that Woodford supplied the welfare-based synthesis. I do not treat the convergence of names as merit. I judge the argument behind it, and I find that the three roles are separable and load-bearing. On my own criteria, theory and evidence developing together, durability and breadth, B014 is at least as strong as B047. The policy rule is an observable, estimable object, and the framework has been used and challenged in practice for decades. It has been extended rather than abandoned after 2008, the zero lower bound and the 2021-23 inflation. Its influence on central-bank practice is also larger than that of any other shortlisted work. Once I count the omissions honestly, B047 has an attribution cost of its own (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are outside the names, and the Krugman 2008 overlap remains). That cost is comparable in kind to B014's exclusion of Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans and Smets. The two entries no longer differ on attribution as I thought in round 1, so breadth of influence decides it. I propose a citation limited to nominal rigidities, policy rules and the micro-founded theory of policy. It does not claim the estimated-DSGE tradition, which keeps the stated scope honest.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution. Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (identifying monetary shocks and the medium-scale model), Smets and Wouters, Galí and Gertler made contributions that made the framework usable in central banks. A three-person cap cannot credit them, and a narrow citation reduces the problem without removing it. A second reservation is that Calvo's pricing device is compact, and Boppart and Fredriksson ask fairly whether a modelling device is a discovery in the sense the Committee normally rewards. I think it is, because so much of the later literature rests on it, but the question is open. A third is maturity and framing. Representative-agent versions are widely seen as being superseded by heterogeneous-agent work, and the 2021-23 inflation is contested. A prize could then reward a stage of the field rather than its end state. Finally, I am moving from my round-1 first choice, B047, whose firm-level evidence I still rate very highly. If the Committee judges the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority issue and the Krugman 2008 overlap to be manageable in a citation, the case for B047 is as strong as the case for B014 on empirical confirmation. I am not verifying priority claims independently.

responses.point: Krusell argues that Calvo (pricing friction), Taylor (contracts and rule) and Woodford (synthesis) are the most distinct conceptual steps, and that the nominal-rigidity and policy-rule core has not been recognised by earlier macro prizes. He accepts that excluding Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost.
responses.response: In round 1 I questioned this because the trios were unstable, and the question was fair to ask then. His account of the three roles, and the fact that members who started from Galí arrived at the same trio for structural reasons, answer most of that objection. I agree with his point that earlier prizes (rational expectations, time consistency, identification, banking crises) did not reward the pricing friction and the rule. I still do not think the exclusion cost is small. I accept the narrower scope of the citation as the way to handle it, and not as a full solution.

responses.point: Fredriksson moved from Woodford, Galí and Taylor to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford because the case rests on nominal rigidities. He wants citation wording that does not claim the estimated-DSGE tradition, and he asks whether Calvo's compact device is a discovery in the sense the Committee normally rewards.
responses.response: I adopt his wording constraint: the citation names pricing and contract frictions, policy rules and the micro-founded theory of policy, and says nothing of estimation. On whether Calvo's device counts as a discovery, I think it does, because it made a forward-looking, tractable Phillips curve possible and almost every later model inherits it. I recognise that this is a judgement about originality and influence, and Galí's case becomes the natural swap if the Committee weights the empirical framework more heavily. In my view that would change the citation's focus and not repair the attribution.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers B003 (Kiyotaki and Moore) for its single-mechanism attribution, and says he would support B014 only if the Committee can agree a defensible narrower citation. He also states that B014 has the larger footprint in practice.
responses.response: I agree that B003 has the cleaner attribution. I also agree with his distinction between the collateral mechanism and the 2022 recognition, so B003 is my second alternative and I would not oppose it. The condition he sets is one I try to meet: the citation specifies three things (pricing and contract frictions, the policy rule and the micro-founded policy theory) and does not claim the whole New Keynesian programme. I rank B014 ahead of B003 on breadth of influence and durability in use. Kiyotaki-Moore has thinner direct empirical identification in the original paper, and I would not call that gap decisive.

responses.point: Boppart, who shares my B047 preference, ranks B014 second but doubts that a trio can carry the discovery. He notes that Calvo's and Taylor's older contract-pricing and rule insights differ from the Woodford-Galí synthesis, so the Committee must say what it credits. He also says timing since 2008 is not scientific merit.
responses.response: I agree that timing since 2008 is not merit, and I leave my favourable-timing remark out of my present reasoning. On his main point I now partly disagree. The citation I propose says what it credits: the older frictions and rule on one side and the synthesis on the other, with Woodford credited for connecting them. That can be a coherent award, not a mixed one, because the synthesis depends on the frictions. I remain with him on B047's merits. The selection and extensive-margin results are a clear step beyond what Krugman's prize recognised, and B047 is my first alternative. Where I change is that B047 has its own priority cost (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum), which I think narrows the attribution difference I stressed in round 1.

uncertainties: Whether a three-name, narrower citation can avoid implicitly ranking Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets, Wouters and Gertler below the three named. I think it reduces the problem but do not think it solves it.

Whether Calvo or Galí should be the third name. I rely on the argument that the pricing friction is the primitive. If the Committee weights the empirical framework more heavily, a Galí swap is defensible.
How much weight the post-2021 inflation and the heterogeneous-agent critique should have on maturity. I read them as extension, but I have no specific observation that would settle it.

Whether B047 would reach a majority if its priority and Krugman-overlap concerns were addressed in a Melitz-Helpman citation. My move from it rests on a judgement of breadth of influence, which is not decisive.
How consistently to apply prior-prize overlap (2022, 2024, 2008, 2005-2020 game theory) across entries. I have not resolved this, and my views on it are provisional.
My assessments rely on background knowledge of the literature and were not independently verified against primary sources.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in economic history (regional growth, railways, electrification, historical national accounts), and none of my listed co-authors is a credited name on any shortlisted entry, including Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. I have no field expertise in monetary macroeconomics, so I rely on the common criteria and on the arguments in the round-1 files. Tommy Andersson is a Lund colleague and a B014 supporter, but the profile shows no co-authorship or candidate link, and I do not treat agreement with him as evidence of merit. My 2023 and 2025 public roles for the Academy do not indicate a private preference. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
